seoDesc: Relative strength index (RSI): work out your result from the period and the price 1. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
Supply the period, the price 1, the price 2 and the price 3 and the Relative strength index (RSI) calculator solves for the answer. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender.

Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Relative strength index (RSI) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Relative strength index (RSI) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the period, the price 1, the price 2 and the price 3.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Relative strength index (RSI) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the period, the price 1 and the price 2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• If a field is empty the result waits rather than guessing: no zero is quietly substituted in the background.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Relative strength index (RSI) calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.
  • There is nothing to invert here: the result is produced in one direction only, from the values you supply.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — period for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Relative strength index (RSI) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the period, the price 1, the price 2 and the price 3, which is 53 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Is the Relative strength index (RSI) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.

faq.q: Does it work in both directions?
faq.a: Where the maths allows it, yes: the page states which values it solves for and which you supply. A field marked as a result is always computed, never typed into.
